Israel dwelt in all the cities--</hi>after exterminating the inhabitants who had been previously doomed (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.34">De 2:34</reference>). <div eID="gen1986" type="x-p"/>
entries.64880462b9d67b987b2a19c736c91c2ffd5e83ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1481"/><div sID="gen1987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1481"/><hi type="bold">26. Heshbon--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.7.4">So 7:4</reference>)--situated sixteen English miles north of the Arnon, and from its ruins it appears to have been a large city. <div eID="gen1987" type="x-p"/>
entries.3da4ca71bddb1f5a8fdd560eb09fa4853ccabf90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1482"/><div sID="gen1988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1482"/><hi type="bold">27-30. Wherefore they that speak in proverbs--</hi>Here is given an extract from an Amorite song exultingly anticipating an extension of their conquests to Arnon. The quotation from the poem of the Amorite bard ends at <reference osisRef="Num.21.28">Nu 21:28</reference>. The two following verses appear to be the strains in which the Israelites expose the impotence of the usurpers. <div eID="gen1988" type="x-p"/>
entries.335861616de908251be11db9196af96cc1b96aa3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1484"/><div sID="gen1991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1484"/><hi type="bold">33. they turned and went up by the way of Bashan--</hi>a name given to that district from the richness of the soil--now Batanea or El-Bottein--a hilly region east of the Jordan lying between the mountains of Hermon on the north and those of Gilead on the south.<div eID="gen1991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Og--</hi>a giant, an Amoritish prince, who, having opposed the progress of the Israelites, was defeated. <div eID="gen1992" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e35772ea24a2c2596e7e3ed3a2994ea695dbfb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1485"/><div sID="gen1993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1485"/><hi type="bold">34-35. The Lord said unto Moses, Fear him not--</hi>a necessary encouragement, for Og's gigantic stature (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.11">De 3:11</reference>) was calculated to inspire terror. He and all his were put to the sword. <chapter eID="Num.21"/>

entries.00ba8b0c138a4a7dcd60b24abcd0d58b47290e78: <div eID="gen5804" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen5805" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5806" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5806" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5805" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5807" type="x-p"/> Arad, a king of the Canaanites, attacks Israel, and makes same prisoners, <reference osisRef="Num.21.1">Num 21:1</reference>. They devote him and his people to destruction, <reference osisRef="Num.21.2">Num 21:2</reference>; which they afterwards accomplished, <reference osisRef="Num.21.3">Num 21:3</reference>. They journey from Hor, and are greatly discouraged, <reference osisRef="Num.21.4">Num 21:4</reference>. They murmur against God and Moses, and loathe the manna, <reference osisRef="Num.21.5">Num 21:5</reference>. The Lord sends fiery serpents among them, <reference osisRef="Num.21.6">Num 21:6</reference>. They repent, and beg Moses to intercede for them, <reference osisRef="Num.21.7">Num 21:7</reference>. The Lord directs him to make a brazen serpent, and set it on a pole, that the people might look on it and be healed, <reference osisRef="Num.21.8">Num 21:8</reference>. Moses does so, and the people who beheld the brazen serpent lived, <reference osisRef="Num.21.9">Num 21:9</reference>. They journey to Oboth, Ije-abarim, Zared, and Arnon, <reference osisRef="Num.21.10-Num.21.13">Num 21:10-13</reference>. A quotation from the book of the wars of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Num.21.14">Num 21:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.21.15">Num 21:15</reference>. From Arnon they came to Beer, <reference osisRef="Num.21.16">Num 21:16</reference>. Their song of triumph, <reference osisRef="Num.21.17-Num.21.20">Num 21:17-20</reference>. Moses sends messengers to the Amorites for permission to pass through their land, <reference osisRef="Num.21.21">Num 21:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.21.22">Num 21:22</reference>. Sihon their king refuses, attacks Israel, is defeated, and all his cities destroyed, <reference osisRef="Num.21.23-Num.21.26">Num 21:23-26</reference>. The poetic proverbs made on the occasion, <reference osisRef="Num.21.27-Num.21.30">Num 21:27-30</reference>. Israel possesses the land of the Amorites, <reference osisRef="Num.21.31">Num 21:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.21.32">Num 21:32</reference>. They are attacked by Og king of Bashan, <reference osisRef="Num.21.33">Num 21:33</reference>. They defeat him, destroy his troops and family, and possess his land, <reference osisRef="Num.21.34">Num 21:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.21.35">Num 21:35</reference>. <div eID="gen5807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5808" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen5808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5809" type="x-p"/> The way of the spies - אתרים atharim. Some think that this signifies the way that the spies took when they went to search the land. But this is impossible, as Dr. Kennicott justly remarks, because Israel had now marched from Meribah-Kadesh to Mount Hor, beyond Ezion-Gaber, and were turning round Edom to the south-east; and therefore the word is to be understood here as the name of a place.
entries.a355bf3bccdb62c1203749327039ad39343e1679: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen5809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5810" type="x-p"/> The Lord hearkened to the voice of Israel - The whole of this verse appears to me to have been added after the days of Joshua. It is certain the Canaanites were not utterly destroyed at the time here spoken of, for this did not take place till after the death of Moses. If, instead of utterly destroyed them, ויחרם vaiyacharem, we translate they devoted them to utter destruction, it will make a good sense, and not repugnant to the Hebrew; though some think it more probable that the verse was added afterwards by Joshua or Ezra, in testimony of the fulfillment of God's promise; for Arad, who is mentioned as being destroyed here, is mentioned among those destroyed by Joshua long after, (see <reference osisRef="Jos.12.14">Jos 12:14</reference>): but this is quite consistent with their being devoted to destruction, as this might be fulfilled any time after. See the note on Leviticus 27 (note).
entries.73c28c5d50ac1f03fffefa2b3c3c4ccb898c64ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen5810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5811" type="x-p"/> This light bread - הקלקל hakkelokel, a word of excessive scorn; as if they had said, This innutritive, unsubstantial, cheat - stomach stuff.
entries.0363324894dbb981430a010e9b047020447c1dfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen5811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5812" type="x-p"/> Fiery serpents - הנחשים השרפים hannechashim hasseraphim. I have observed before, on Gen. iii., that it is difficult to assign a name to the creature termed in Hebrew nachash; it has different significations, but its meaning here and in Gen. iii. is most difficult to be ascertained. Seraphim is one of the orders of angelic beings, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.2">Isa 6:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.6">Isa 6:6</reference>; but as it comes from the root שרף saraph, which signifies to burn, it has been translated fiery in the text. It is likely that St. Paul alludes to the seraphim, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.7">Heb 1:7</reference> : Who maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a Flame Of Fire. The animals mentioned here by Moses may have been called fiery because of the heat, violent inflammation, and thirst, occasioned by their bite; and consequently, if serpents, they were of the prester or dipsas species, whose bite, especially that of the former, occasioned a violent inflammation through the whole body, and a fiery appearance of the countenance. The poet Lucan has well expressed this terrible effect of the bite of the prester, and also of the dipsas, in the ninth book of his Pharsalia, which, for the sake of those who may not have the work at hand, I shall here insert. <div eID="gen5812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5813" type="x-p"/> Of the mortal effects of the bite of the dipsas in the deserts of Libya he gives the following description: - "Signiferum juvenem Tyrrheni sanguinis Aulum <div eID="gen5813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5814" type="x-p"/> Torta caput retro dipsas calcata momordit. <div eID="gen5814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5815" type="x-p"/> Vix dolor aut sensus dentis fuit: ipsaque laeti <div eID="gen5815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5816" type="x-p"/> Frons caret invidia: nec quidquam plaga minatur. <div eID="gen5816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5817" type="x-p"/> Ecce subit virus tacitum, carpitque medullas <div eID="gen5817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5818" type="x-p"/> Ignis edax, calidaque incendit viscera tabe. <div eID="gen5818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5819" type="x-p"/> Ebibit humorem circum vitalia fusum <div eID="gen5819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5820" type="x-p"/> Pestis, et in sicco linguam torrere palato <div eID="gen5820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5821" type="x-p"/> Coepit: defessos iret qui sudor in artus <div eID="gen5821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5822" type="x-p"/> Non fuit, atque oculos lacrymarum vena refugit." <div eID="gen5822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5823" type="x-p"/> Aulus, a noble youth of Tyrrhene blood, <div eID="gen5823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5824" type="x-p"/> Who bore the standard, on a dipsas trod; <div eID="gen5824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5825" type="x-p"/> Backward the wrathful serpent bent her head, <div eID="gen5825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5826" type="x-p"/> And, fell with rage, the unheeded wrong repaid. <div eID="gen5826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5827" type="x-p"/> Scarce did some little mark of hurt remain, <div eID="gen5827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5828" type="x-p"/> And scarce he found some little sense of pain. <div eID="gen5828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5829" type="x-p"/> Nor could he yet the danger doubt, nor fear <div eID="gen5829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5830" type="x-p"/> That death with all its terrors threatened there. <div eID="gen5830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5831" type="x-p"/> When lo! unseen, the secret venom spreads, <div eID="gen5831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5832" type="x-p"/> And every nobler part at once invades; <div eID="gen5832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5833" type="x-p"/> Swift flames consume the marrow and the brain, <div eID="gen5833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5834" type="x-p"/> And the scorched entrails rage with burning pain; <div eID="gen5834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5835" type="x-p"/> Upon his heart the thirsty poisons prey, <div eID="gen5835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5836" type="x-p"/> And drain the sacred juice of life away. <div eID="gen5836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5837" type="x-p"/> No kindly floods of moisture bathe his tongue, <div eID="gen5837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5838" type="x-p"/> But cleaving to the parched roof it hung; <div eID="gen5838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5839" type="x-p"/> No trickling drops distil, no dewy sweat, <div eID="gen5839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5840" type="x-p"/> To ease his weary limbs, and cool the raging heat. <div eID="gen5840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5841" type="x-p"/> Rowe. <div eID="gen5841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5842" type="x-p"/> The effects of the bite of the prester are not less terrible: "Nasidium Marsi cultorem torridus agri <div eID="gen5842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5843" type="x-p"/> Percussit prester: illi rubor igneus ora <div eID="gen5843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5844" type="x-p"/> Succendit, tenditque cutem, pereunte figura, <div eID="gen5844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5845" type="x-p"/> Miscens cuncta tumor toto jam corpore major: <div eID="gen5845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5846" type="x-p"/> Humanumque egressa modum super omnia membra <div eID="gen5846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5847" type="x-p"/> Effiatur sanies, late tollente veneno." <div eID="gen5847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5848" type="x-p"/> A fate of different kind Nasidius found, <div eID="gen5848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5849" type="x-p"/> A burning prester gave the deadly wound; <div eID="gen5849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5850" type="x-p"/> And straight, a sudden flame began to spread, <div eID="gen5850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5851" type="x-p"/> And paint his visage with a glowing red. <div eID="gen5851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5852" type="x-p"/> With swift expansion swells the bloated skin. <div eID="gen5852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5853" type="x-p"/> Naught but an undistinguished mass is seen; <div eID="gen5853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5854" type="x-p"/> While the fair human form lies lost within. <div eID="gen5854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5855" type="x-p"/> The puffy poison spreads, and leaves around, <div eID="gen5855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5856" type="x-p"/> Till all the man is in the monster drowned. <div eID="gen5856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5857" type="x-p"/> Rowe. <div eID="gen5857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5858" type="x-p"/> Bochart supposes that the hydrus or chersydrus is meant; a serpent that lives in marshy places, the bite of which produces the most terrible inflammations, burning heat, fetid vomitings, and a putrid solution of the whole body. See his works, vol. iii., col. 421. It is more likely to have been a serpent of the prester or dipsas kind, as the wilderness through which the Israelites passed did neither afford rivers nor marshes, though Bochart endeavors to prove that there might have been marshes in that part; but his arguments have very little weight. Nor is there need of a water serpent as long as the prester or dipsas, which abound in the deserts of Libya, might have abounded in the deserts of Arabia also. But very probably the serpents themselves were immediately sent by God for the chastisement of this rebellious people. The cure was certainly preternatural; this no person doubts; and why might not the agent be so, that inflicted the disease?
entries.911969832b2b509fa999328f3b045c279eac54bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen5858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5859" type="x-p"/> Make thee a fiery serpent - Literally, make thee a seraph. <div eID="gen5859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5860" type="x-p"/> And put it upon a pole - על נס al nes, upon a standard or ensign.
entries.2f4e6652bccef93218e47de2c10aa2eeaf467b52: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen5860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5861" type="x-p"/> And Moses made a serpent of brass - נחש נחשת nechash nechosheth. Hence we find that the word for brass or copper comes from the same root with nachash, which here signifies a serpent, probably on account of the color; as most serpents, especially those of the bright spotted kind, have a very glistening appearance, and those who have brown or yellow spots appear something like burnished brass: but the true meaning of the root cannot be easily ascertained. On the subject of the cure of the serpent-bitten Israelites, by looking at the brazen serpent, there is a good comment in the book of The Wisdom of Solomon, (Apoch). <reference osisRef="Num.16.4-Num.16.12">Num 16:4-12</reference>, in which are these remarkable words: "They were admonished, having a sign of salvation, (i. e., the brazen serpent), to put them in remembrance of the commandments of thy law. For he that turned himself towards it was not saved by the Thing that he saw, but by Thee, that art the Savior of all." To the circumstance of looking at the brazen serpent in order to be healed, our Lord refers, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.14">Joh 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.15">Joh 3:15</reference> : "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life." The brazen serpent was certainly no type of Jesus Christ; but from our Lord's words we may learn, <div eID="gen5861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5862" type="x-p"/> 1. That as the serpent was lifted up on the pole or ensign, so Jesus Christ was lifted up on the cross. <div eID="gen5862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5863" type="x-p"/> 2. That as the Israelites were to look at the brazen serpent, so sinners must look to Christ for salvation. <div eID="gen5863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5864" type="x-p"/> 3. That as God provided no other remedy than this looking for the wounded Israelites, so he has provided no other way of salvation than faith in the blood of his Son. <div eID="gen5864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5865" type="x-p"/> 4. That as he who looked at the brazen serpent was cured and did live, so he that believeth on the Lord Jesus Christ shall not perish, but have eternal life. <div eID="gen5865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5866" type="x-p"/> 5. That as neither the serpent, nor looking at it, but the invisible power of God healed the people, so neither the cross of Christ, nor his merely being crucified, but the pardon he has bought by his blood, communicated by the powerful energy of his Spirit, saves the souls of men. <div eID="gen5866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5867" type="x-p"/> May not all these things be plainly seen in the circumstances of this transaction, without making the serpent a type of Jesus Christ, (the most exceptionable that could possibly be chosen), and running the parallel, as some have done, through ten or a dozen particulars?
entries.2c1e99f9fb1881788f441afc056534cf89cb092c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen5867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5868" type="x-p"/> They - pitched in the valley of Zared - נחל זרד nachal zared. This should be translated the brook Zared, as it is in <reference osisRef="Deu.2.13">Deu 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.2.14">Deu 2:14</reference>. This stream has its origin in the mountains eastward of Moab, and runs from east to west, and discharges itself into the Dead Sea.
entries.bdadd70107d5422b16cc01f59097443042f98dd1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen5868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5869" type="x-p"/> Arnon - Another river which takes its rise in the mountains of Moab, and, after having separated the ancient territories of the Moabites and Ammonites, falls into the Dead Sea, near the mouth of Jordan.
entries.f222d5e818be4d2b678f81a2342b910f704a2de1: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen5869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5870" type="x-p"/> The book of the wars of the Lord - There are endless conjectures about this book, both among ancients and moderns. Dr. Lightfoot's opinion is the most simple, and to me bears the greatest appearance of being the true one. "This book seems to have been some book of remembrances and directions, written by Moses for Joshua's private instruction for the management of the wars after him. See <reference osisRef="Exo.17.14-Exo.17.16">Exo 17:14-16</reference>. It may be that this was the same book which is called the book of Jasher, i. e., the book of the upright, or a directory for Joshua, from Moses, what to do and what to expect in his wars; and in this book it seems as if Moses directed the setting up of archery, see <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.18">2Sam 1:18</reference>, and warrants Joshua to command the sun, and expect its obedience, <reference osisRef="Jos.10.13">Jos 10:13</reference>." <div eID="gen5870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5871" type="x-p"/> What he did in the Red Sea, and in the brooks of Arnon - This clause is impenetrably obscure. All the versions, all the translators, and all the commentators, have been puzzled with it. Scarcely any two agree. The original is את והב בסופה eth vaheb besuphah, which our translators render, what he did in the Red Sea, following here the Chaldee Targum; but not satisfied with this version, they have put the most difficult words in English letters in the margin, Vaheb in Suphah. Calmet's conjecture here is ingenious, and is adopted by Houbigant; instead of והב vaheb, he reads זרד zared. Now a ז zain may be easily mistaken for a ו vau, and vice versa; and a ה he for a ר, resh, if the left limb happened to be a little obliterated, which frequently occurs, not only in MSS., but in printed books; the ב beth also might be mistaken for a ד daleth, if the ruled line on which it stood happened in that place to be a little thicker or blacker than usual. Thus then והב vaheb might be easily formed out of זרד zared, mentioned <reference osisRef="Num.21.12">Num 21:12</reference>; the whole might then be read, They encamped at the brook Zared, and they came to Suphah, and thence to the brook Arnon. Take the passage as we may, it is evidently defective. As I judge the whole clause to have been a common proverb in those days, and Vaheb to be a proper name, I therefore propose the following translation, which I believe to be the best: From Vaheb unto Suph, and unto the streams of Arnon. If we allow it to have been a proverbial expression, used to point out extensive distance, then it was similar to that well known phrase, From Dan even unto Beersheba.
entries.e34ede369273aa55b3975a7f7c25294bb6c58c1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen5871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5872" type="x-p"/> Spring up, O well, etc. - This is one of the most ancient war songs in the world, but is not easily understood, which is commonly the case with all very ancient compositions, especially the poetic. See the remarks <reference osisRef="Exo.15.1">Exo 15:1</reference> (note), etc.
entries.0dcaff5bdbe58400e97d60cbb6d5867004113537: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen5872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5873" type="x-p"/> The princes digged the well - with their staves - This is not easily understood. Who can suppose that the princes dug this well with their staves? And is there any other idea conveyed by our translation? The word חפרו chapharu, which is translated they digged, should be rendered they searched out, which is a frequent meaning of the root; and במשענתם bemishanotham, which we render with their staves, should be translated on their borders or confines, from the root שען shaan, to lie along. With these corrections the whole song may be read thus: - <div eID="gen5873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5874" type="x-p"/> Spring up, O well! Answer ye to it. <div eID="gen5874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5875" type="x-p"/> The well, the princes searched it out. <div eID="gen5875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5876" type="x-p"/> The nobles of the people have digged it. <div eID="gen5876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5877" type="x-p"/> By a decree, upon their own borders <div eID="gen5877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5878" type="x-p"/> This is the whole of the quotation from what is called the book of the wars of the Lord. But see Dr. Kennicott's remarks at the end of this chapter.
entries.f476aa1c8a6accd14983b61d06db9451a00bb4dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen5878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5879" type="x-p"/> For Heshbon was the city of Sihon, etc. - It appears therefore that the territory now taken from Sihon by the Israelites was taken from a former king of Moab, in commemoration of which an epikedion or war song was made, several verses of which, in their ancient poetic form, are here quoted by Moses.
entries.2d934d25c492cc6c919fabc4d387c69eab455425: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen5879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5880" type="x-p"/> They that speak in proverbs - המשלים hammoshelim, from משל mashal, to rule, to exercise authority; hence a weighty proverbial saying, because admitted as an axiom for the government of life. The moshelim of the ancient Asiatics were the same, in all probability, as the Poetae among the Greeks and Latins, the shaara among the Arabs, who were esteemed as Divine persons, and who had their name from shaara, he knew, understood; whose poems celebrated past transactions, and especially those which concerned the military history of their nation. These poets were also termed sahebi deewan, companions or lords of the council of state, because their weighty sayings and universal knowledge were held in the highest repute. Similar to these were the bards among the ancient Druids, and the Sennachies among the ancient Celtic inhabitants of these nations. <div eID="gen5880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5881" type="x-p"/> The ode from the 27th to the 30th verse is composed of three parts. The first takes in <reference osisRef="Num.21.27">Num 21:27</reference> and <reference osisRef="Num.21.28">Num 21:28</reference>; the second <reference osisRef="Num.21.29">Num 21:29</reference>; and the third <reference osisRef="Num.21.30">Num 21:30</reference>. <div eID="gen5881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5882" type="x-p"/> The first records with bitter irony the late insults of Sihon and his subjects over the conquered Moabites. <div eID="gen5882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5883" type="x-p"/> The second expresses the compassion of the Israelites over the desolations of Moab, with a bitter sarcasm against their god Chemosh, who had abandoned his votaries in their distress, or was not able to rescue them out of the hands of their enemies. <div eID="gen5883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5884" type="x-p"/> The third sets forth the revenge taken by Israel upon the whole country of Sihon, from Heshbon to Dibon, and from Nophah even to Medeba. See <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Isa 15:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Isa 15:2</reference>. <div eID="gen5884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5885" type="x-p"/> The whole poem, divided into its proper hemistichs, as it stands in Kennicott's Hebrew Bible, is as follows: - <div eID="gen5885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5886" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi>. Part I <div eID="gen5886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5887" type="x-p"/> Come ye to Heshbon, let it be rebuilt; <div eID="gen5887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5888" type="x-p"/> The city of Sihon, let it be established. <div eID="gen5888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5889" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen5889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5890" type="x-p"/> For from Heshbon the fire went out, <div eID="gen5890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5891" type="x-p"/> And a flame from the city of Sihon: <div eID="gen5891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5892" type="x-p"/> It hath consumed the city of Moab, <div eID="gen5892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5893" type="x-p"/> With the lords of the heights of Arnon. <div eID="gen5893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5894" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi>. Part 2 <div eID="gen5894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5895" type="x-p"/> Alas for thee, O Moab! <div eID="gen5895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5896" type="x-p"/> Thou hast perished, O people of Chemosh! <div eID="gen5896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5897" type="x-p"/> He hath given up his fugitive sons <div eID="gen5897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5898" type="x-p"/> And his daughters into captivity, <div eID="gen5898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5899" type="x-p"/> To the king of the Amorites, Sihon. <div eID="gen5899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5900" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi>. Part 3 <div eID="gen5900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5901" type="x-p"/> But on them have We lifted destruction, <div eID="gen5901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5902" type="x-p"/> From Heshbon even to Dibon; <div eID="gen5902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5903" type="x-p"/> We have destroyed even to Nophah, <div eID="gen5903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5904" type="x-p"/> The fire did reach to Medebah. <div eID="gen5904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5905" type="x-p"/> See Kennicott's Remarks.
entries.6070c87c61f468344378c323b54c66402eb92ea4: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen5905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5906" type="x-p"/> So they smote him, and his sons - There is a curious note of Dr. Lightfoot here, of which I should think it wrong to deprive the reader. "Sihon and Og conquered, A. M. 2553. Of the life of Moses, 120. From the Exodus, 40. It is now six and twenty generations from the creation, or from Adam to Moses; and accordingly doth Psalm 136, rehearse the durableness of God's mercy six and twenty times over, beginning the story with the creation, and ending it in the conquest of Sihon and Og. The numerals of the name יהוה Jehovah amount to the sum of six and twenty." <div eID="gen5906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5907" type="x-p"/> On some difficulties in this chapter Dr. Kennicott makes the following observations: - "This one chapter has several very considerable difficulties; and some verses, as now translated, are remarkably unintelligible, A true state of this chapter is not, however, to be despaired of; and it has in it some circumstances which merit more than common attention. It contains the history of the last part of the travels of the Israelites in their way to the promised land; beginning with them at Mount Hor, the thirty-fourth encampment, and concluding with them, as in their forty-second and last encampment, near Jordan, in the country which they had acquired by conquest over Sihon, king of the Amorites. "It begins with saying - that King Arad, the Canaanite, who dwelt in the south, (in the land of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Num.33.40">Num 33:40</reference>), attacked Israel and was defeated, and that Israel destroyed their cities; and that, after destroying these Canaanite cities, and consequently after being in a part of Canaan, a part of the very country they were going to, on the west of the Dead Sea, they returned towards the Red Sea, and near the eastern tongue or gulf of the Red Sea, on the south of Edom, marched round Edom to the east of the Dead Sea, in order to enter Canaan from the east side of Jordan! "This surprising representation of so vast and dangerous a march, quite unnecessarily performed, is owing to two circumstances. The first is, (<reference osisRef="Num.21.1">Num 21:1</reference>), the Canaanites heard that Israel was coming by the way of the spies, meaning, by the way the spies went from Kadesh-Barnea into Canaan. But this being impossible, because Israel had now marched from Meribah-Kadesh to Mount Hor, beyond Ezion-gaber, and were turning round Edom, to the south-east; it is happy that the word rendered spies, in our version, is in the Greek a proper name, (Atharim), which removes that difficulty: and the other difficulty (<reference osisRef="Num.21.2">Num 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.21.3">Num 21:3</reference>) is removed by the Greek version likewise, according to which, the vow made, with the facts subsequent, does not signify destroying the Canaanite cities, but devoting them to destruction at some future time. See Wall's Crit. Notes. "It proceeds with saying, that after defeating the Canaanites at Mount Hor, they journeyed from Mount Hor by the way of the Red Sea, (in the road from Ammon, Midian, etc., to the eastern gulf of the Red Sea), to compass the land of Edom; that on their murmuring for want both of bread and of water they were punished by fiery serpents, after which they marched to Oboth, and thence to Ije-abarim in the wilderness, east of Moab. The encampments of the Israelites, amounting to forty-two, are recorded all together, in historical succession, in Numbers 33, where Ije-abarim is the 38th; Dibon-gad, 39; Almon-Diblathaim, 40; mountains of Abarim, 41; and the plains of Moab, by Jordan, 42. This regular detail in Numbers 33 has occasioned great perplexity as to Numbers 21, where, after the stations at Oboth and Ije-abarim, in <reference osisRef="Num.21.10">Num 21:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.21.11">Num 21:11</reference>, we have, in <reference osisRef="Num.21.19">Num 21:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.21.20">Num 21:20</reference>, the words Mattanah, Nahaliel, and Bamoth; which are usually considered as the proper names of three places, but widely different from the three proper names after Ije-abarim in the catalogue at Numbers 33. "But there is, in reality, no inconsistency here. In the plain and historical catalogue (Numbers 33). the words are strictly the proper names of the three places; but here the words Mattanah, Nahaliel, and Bamoth follow some lines of poetry, and seem to form a continuation of the song. They evidently express figurative and poetical ideas. The verbs journeyed from and pitched in are not found here, though necessary to prose narration: see <reference osisRef="Num.33.10">Num 33:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Num.33.11">Num 33:11</reference> here, and Numbers 33. Lastly, <reference osisRef="Num.21.20">Num 21:20</reference>, (in this 21st chapter), usually supposed to express the last encampment, does not. Pisgah signifies a hill; and the Israelites could not encamp on the top of any single hill, such as this is described. Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which looketh toward Jeshimon, (<reference osisRef="Num.23.28">Num 23:28</reference>), which Peor undoubtedly was in Moab. He took him to another hill in Moab, when he took him (<reference osisRef="Num.23.14">Num 23:14</reference>) to the top of Pisgah, in the field of Zophim. And if the Pisgah or hill in <reference osisRef="Num.21.20">Num 21:20</reference>, was in the country of Balak, it could not point out the last encampment, which was not in Balak's country, but north of Arnon. "The word Mattanah probably alludes to a place distinguished by some gift or blessing from God. Fagius says: <div eID="gen5907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5908" type="x-p"/> Nomen loci, ab eventu aquarum quas Dominus ibi dedit, sic appellati; מתנה nam significat donum- 'The name of the place was so called, from the circumstance of the waters which the Lord gave there; for Mattanah signifies a gift.' נהליאל Nahaliel is torrentes Dei; i. e., great streams, particularly seasonable or salutary. And במות Bamoth (<reference osisRef="Num.21.20">Num 21:20</reference>) may point out any high places of signal benefit in the country of Moab, or it may answer to the last station but one, which was the mountains of Abarim. <div eID="gen5908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5909" type="x-p"/> If, therefore, these words were meant to express poetically some eminent blessing, what blessing was so likely to be then celebrated as copious streams of water? And after they had wandered nearly forty years through many a barren desert, and after (compare <reference osisRef="Deu.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference>) having passed through that great and terrible wilderness, wherein were fiery serpents and drought, where there was no water, it is no wonder they should shout for joy at finding water in plenty, and finding it almost on the banks of Arnon, the last river they were to pass, in their way to their last station, east of Jordan. No wonder they should sing in poetic rapture, that after the wilderness was (Mattanah) the Gift Of God; meaning the great well in Moab, dug by public authority; and no wonder that, after such a gift, there were (Nahaliel) blessed streams, by which they passed, till they came to (Bamoth) the high places from which, perhaps, these streams descended. And the thanksgiving ends, where the blessing was no longer wanted, on their coming down into the valley, along the banks of Arnon, which was then the north boundary of Moab. "The Israelites had spent no less than thirty-eight years in coming from Kadesh-Barnea to their encampment north of Zared. Here, at this fortieth station, they were commanded to pass through Moab by ער Ar, the chief city; but were not to stop till they came to the valley on the south of Arnon. At this last station but one they probably continued no longer than was necessary for sending messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, at Heshbon, and receiving his answer. They then crossed the Arnon; and having vanquished Sihon and Og, took possession of the forty-second and last encampment. "This one chapter has three pieces of poetry, either fragments or complete; and poetry, seldom found in a historical narrative, may be here accounted for from the exuberance of joy which must have affected these wearied travelers, when arriving thus happily near their journey's end. What occurs first is in <reference osisRef="Num.21.14">Num 21:14</reference>; and has often been called the fragment of an old Amorite song. But it may have been Amorite or Moabite, or either or neither, for the subject matter of it, as it is generally understood, if indeed it can be said to be understood at all. The words את והב בסופה ואת הנתליס ארנו, usually supposed to contain this fragment, do not signify, as in our English version, What he did in the Red Sea, and in the brooks of Arnon. Without enumerating the many interpretations given by others, I shall offer a new one, which seems to make good sense, and a sense very pertinent. "Observe first, that there must have been a place called Suph, near the conflux of the Arnon and Jordan; because Moses, whilst in that last station, begins Deuteronomy with saying, he was on this side (i. e., east) of Jordan, over against Suph. By this word is not here meant the Red Sea; partly, because that has every where else the word for sea before it, and partly, because of the great distance of the Red Sea now from Moses. The single word, therefore, signifies here some place in itself obscure, because no where mentioned but in these two passages. And yet we cannot wonder that Moses should mention it twice, as the word Suph, introduced in speaking of the two last encampments, recalled to mind the Sea of Suph, so glorious to Israel, near the beginning of their march towards Canaan. "Moses had now led Israel from the Red Sea to the river Arnon, through many dreadful dangers, partly from hostile nations, partly from themselves; such dangers as no other people ever experienced, and such as no people could have surmounted, without the signal favor of the Almighty. And here, just before the battles with Sihon and Og, he reminds them of Pharaoh, etc.; and he asserts, that in the history of the wars it shall be recorded that Jehovah, who had triumphantly brought Israel through the Sea of Suph, near Egypt, at first, had now conducted him to Suph, near Arnon; that <div eID="gen5909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5910" type="x-p"/> Jehovah went with him to Suph, <div eID="gen5910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5911" type="x-p"/> And he came to the streams of Arnon. "This version removes the difficulties urged by Hobbes, page 266, fol. 1750; by Spinoza, page 108, 4th., 1670; and retailed in a deistical pamphlet called The Doubts of the Infidels, page 4, 8vo., 1781. "The general meaning of the next piece of poetry seems to be this: that at some distance from the city of Ar, by which the Israelites were to pass, (<reference osisRef="Deu.2.18">Deu 2:18</reference>), they came to A Well of uncommon size and magnificence, which seems to have been sought out, built up, and adorned for the public, by the rulers of Moab. And it is no wonder that, on their arrival at such a well, they should look upon it as a blessing from Heaven, and speak of it as a new miracle in their favor. <div eID="gen5911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5912" type="x-p"/> 17. Then Israel sang this song: - Spring up, O Well! Sing ye hitherto! <div eID="gen5912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5913" type="x-p"/> 18. The Well! princes searched it out;The nobles of the people have digged it;By their decree, by their act of government,So, after the wilderness, was Mattanah! <div eID="gen5913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5914" type="x-p"/> 19. And after Mattanah were Nahaliel!And after Nahaliel were Bamoth! <div eID="gen5914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5915" type="x-p"/> 20. And after Bamoth was the valley;Where, in the country of Moab, Appeareth the top of Pisgah,Which is over against Jeshimon. <div eID="gen5915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5916" type="x-p"/> See Dr. Kennicott's Remarks upon Select Passages in the Old Testament.  <chapter eID="Num.21"/> <div eID="gen5916" type="x-p"/>

entries.89b55644add109d10aac621740219f5b875927ac: Num 21:1-3 <div eID="gen1869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1870" type="x-p"/> Victory of Israel over the Canaanitish King of Arad. - When this Canaanitish king, who dwelt in the Negeb, i.e., the south of Palestine (vid., Num 13:17), heard that Israel was coming the way of the spies, he made war upon the Israelites, and took some of them prisoners. <hi type="italic">Arad</hi> is mentioned both here and in the parallel passage, Num 33:40, and also by the side of <hi type="italic">Hormah</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Josh.12.14">Jos 12:14</reference>, as the seat of a Canaanitish king (cf. Jdg 1:16-17). According to <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Onomast</hi>., it was twenty Roman miles to the south of Hebron, and has been preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Tell Arad</hi>, which v. Schubert (ii. pp. 457ff.) and Robinson (ii. pp. 473, 620, and 624) saw in the distance; and, according to <hi type="italic">Roth</hi> in <hi type="italic">Petermann's</hi> geographische Mittheilungen (1858, p. 269), it was situated to the south-east of Kurmul (Carmel), in an undulating plain, without trees or shrubs, with isolated hills and ranges of hills in all directions, among which was <hi type="italic">Tell Arad</hi>. The meaning of האתרים שדרך is uncertain. The lxx, <hi type="italic">Saad</hi>., and others, take the word <hi type="italic">Atharim</hi> as the proper name of a place not mentioned again; but the <hi type="italic">Chaldee</hi>, <hi type="italic">Samar</hi>., and <hi type="italic">Syr</hi>. render it with much greater probability as an appellative noun formed from תּוּר with א <hi type="italic">prosthet</hi>., and synonymous with התּרים, the spies (Num 14:6). The way of the spies was the way through the desert of Zin, which the Israelitish spies had previously taken to Canaan (Num 13:21). The territory of the king of Arad extended to the southern frontier of Canaan, to the desert of Zin, through which the Israelites went from Kadesh to Mount Hor. The Canaanites attacked them when upon their march, and made some of them prisoners.
entries.36cef58621fa385e6ba46761fb38d295309c41b8: Num 21:4-9 <div eID="gen1871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1872" type="x-p"/> March of Israel through the Arabah. Plague of Serpents, and Brazen Serpent. - Num 21:4. As the Edomites refused a passage through their land when the Israelites left Mount Hor, they were obliged to take the way to the Red Sea, in order to go round the land of Edom, that is to say, to go down the Arabah to the head of the Elanitic Gulf.
entries.d2930cc879c954c7212036425824b7b887ef9c96: Num 21:10-20 <div eID="gen1878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1879" type="x-p"/> March of Israel round Edom and Moab, to the Heights of Pisgah in the Field of Moab (cf. Num 33:41-47). - Num 21:10. From the camp in the Arabah, which is not more particularly described, where the murmuring people were punished by fiery serpents, Israel removed to <hi type="italic">Oboth</hi>. According to the list of stations in Num 33:41., they went from Hor to <hi type="italic">Zalmonah</hi>, the situation of which has not been determined; for <hi type="italic">C. v. Raumer's</hi> conjecture (<hi type="italic">der Zug der Israeliten, </hi>p. 45), that it was the same place as the modern <hi type="italic">Maan</hi>, has no firm basis in the fact that Maan is a station of the Syrian pilgrim caravans. From <hi type="italic">Zalmonah</hi> they went to <hi type="italic">Phunon</hi>, and only then to <hi type="italic">Oboth</hi>. The name <hi type="italic">Phunon</hi> is no doubt the same as <hi type="italic">Phinon</hi>, a tribe-seat of the Edomitish Phylarch (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.41">Gen 36:41</reference>); and according to <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> (<hi type="italic">Onom. s. v. Fenon</hi>), it was “a little village in the desert, where copper was dug up by condemned criminals (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.36.41">Gen 36:41</reference>), between Petra and Zoar.” This statement suits very well, provided we imagine the situation of Phunon to have been not in a straight line between Petra and Zoar, but more to the east, between the mountains on the edge of the desert. For the Israelites unquestionably went from the southern end of the Arabah to the eastern side of Idumaea, through the Wady <hi type="italic">el Ithm</hi> (<hi type="italic">Getum</hi>), which opens into the Arabah from the east, a few hours to the north of Akaba and the ancient Ezion-geber. They had then gone round the mountains of Edom, and begun to “turn to the north” (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.3">Deu 2:3</reference>), so that they now proceeded farther northwards, on the eastern side of the mountains of Edom, “through the territory of the sons of Esau,” no doubt by the same road which is taken in the present day by the caravans which go from Gaza to Maan, through the Ghor. “This runs upon a grassy ridge, forming the western border of the coast of Arabia, and the eastern border of the cultivated land, which stretches from the land of Edom to the sources of the Jordan, on the eastern side of the Ghor” (v. <hi type="italic">Raumer</hi>, Zug, p. 45). On the western side of their mountains the Edomites had refused permission to the Israelites to pass through their land (Num 20:18.), as the mountains of Seir terminate towards the Ghor (the Arabah) in steep and lofty precipices, and there are only two or three narrow wadys which intersect them from west to east; and of these the Wady Ghuweir is the only one which is practicable for an army, and even this could be held so securely by a moderate army, that no enemy could force its way into the heart of the country (see <hi type="italic">Leake</hi> in <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, pp. 21, 22; and Robinson, ii. p. 583). It was different on the eastern side, where the mountains slope off into a wide extent of table-land, which is only slightly elevated above the desert of Arabia. Here, on the weaker side of their frontier, the Edomites lost the heart to make any attack upon the Israelites, who would now have been able to requite their hostilities. But the Lord had commanded Israel not to make war upon the sons of Esau; but when passing through their territory, to purchase food and water from them for money (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.4-Deut.2.6">Deu 2:4-6</reference>). The Edomites submitted to the necessity, and endeavoured to take advantage of it, by selling provisions, “in the same way in which, at the present day, the caravan from Mecca is supplied with provisions by the inhabitants of the mountains along the pilgrim road” (<hi type="italic">Leake</hi> in <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, p. 24). The situation of Oboth cannot be determined.
entries.b54e7da30bdfae54ad9c48fe4eb5bc2c8c6d6ca9: Num 21:21-23 <div eID="gen1889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1890" type="x-p"/> When the Israelites reached the eastern border of the kingdom of the Amorite king <hi type="italic">Sihon</hi> (see at Num 21:13), they sent messengers to him, as they had previously done to the king of Edom, to ask permission to pass peaceably through his territory upon the high road (cf. Num 21:22 and Num 20:17); and Sihon refused this request, just as the king of Edom had done, and marched with all his people against the Israelites. But whereas the Lord forbade the Israelites to make war upon their kinsmen the Edomites, He now commanded them to make war upon the Amorite king, and take possession of his land (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.24-Deut.2.25">Deu 2:24-25</reference>); for the Amorites belonged to the Canaanitish tribes which were ripe for the judgment of extermination (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Gen 15:16</reference>). And if, notwithstanding this, the Israelites sent to him with words of peace (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.26">Deu 2:26</reference>), this was simply done to leave the decision of his fate in his own hand (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.2.24">Deu 2:24</reference>). Sihon came out against the Israelites into the desert as far as <hi type="italic">Jahza</hi>, where a battle was fought, in which he was defeated. The accounts of the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. concerning Jahza, which was situated, according to <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi>, between <hi type="italic">Medamon</hi> (<hi type="italic">Medaba</hi>) and <hi type="italic">Debous</hi> (<hi type="italic">Dibon</hi>, see above), and according to Jerome, between <hi type="italic">Medaba</hi> and <hi type="italic">Deblatai</hi>, may be reconciled with the statement that it was in the desert, provided we assume that it was not in a straight line between the places named, but in a more easterly direction on the edge of the desert, near to the commencement of the Wady <hi type="italic">Wale</hi>, a conclusion to which the juxtaposition of <hi type="italic">Jahza</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mephaot</hi> in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.18">Jos 13:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.37">Jos 21:37</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.48.21">Jer 48:21</reference>, also points (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.13.18">Jos 13:18</reference>).
entries.55733da794614117950937206d72fa6f213376b3: Num 21:24-26 <div eID="gen1890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1891" type="x-p"/> Israel smote him with the edge of the sword, i.e., without quarter (see <reference osisRef="Gen.34.26">Gen 34:26</reference>), and took possession of his land “<hi type="italic">from Arnon (Mojeb) to the Jabbok, unto the children of Ammon,”</hi> i.e., to the upper Jabbok, the modern <hi type="italic">Nahr or Moiet Ammân</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Jabbok</hi>, now called <hi type="italic">Zerka</hi>, i.e., the blue, does not take its rise, as <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi> supposed, on the pilgrim-road by the castle of <hi type="italic">Zerka</hi>; but its source, according to <hi type="italic">Abulfeda</hi> <hi type="italic">(tab. Syr.</hi> p. 91) and <hi type="italic">Buckingham</hi>, is the <hi type="italic">Nahr</hi> <hi type="italic">Ammân</hi>, which flowed down from the ancient capital of the Ammonites, and was called the <hi type="italic">upper Jabbok</hi>, and formed the western border of the Ammonites towards the kingdom of Sihon, and subsequently towards Gad (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.37">Deu 2:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.16">Deu 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.12.2">Jos 12:2</reference>). “<hi type="italic">For the border of the Ammonites was strong”</hi> (firm), i.e., strongly fortified; “for which reason Sihon had only been able to push his conquests to the upper Jabbok, not into the territory of the Ammonites.” This explanation of <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> is perfectly correct; since the reason why the Israelites did not press forward into the country of the Ammonites, was not the strength of their frontier, but the word of the Lord, “Make not war upon them, for I shall give thee no possession of the land of the children of Ammon” (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.19">Deu 2:19</reference>). God had only promised the patriarchs, on behalf of their posterity, that He would give them the land of Canaan, which was bounded towards the east by the Jordan (Num 34:2-12; compared with <reference osisRef="Gen.10.19">Gen 10:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.15.19-Gen.15.21">Gen 15:19-21</reference>); and the Israelites would have received no settlement at all on the eastern side of the Jordan, had not the Canaanitish branch of the Amorites extended itself to that side in the time of Moses, and conquered a large portion of the possessions of the Moabites, and also (according to <reference osisRef="Josh.13.25">Jos 13:25</reference>, as compared with Jdg 11:13) of the Ammonites, driving back the Moabites as far as the Arnon, and the Ammonites behind the <hi type="italic">Nahr Ammân</hi>. With the defeat of the Amorites, all the land that they had conquered passed into the possession of the Israelites, who took possession of these towns (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.2.34-Deut.2.36">Deu 2:34-36</reference>). The statement in Num 21:25, that Israel settled in all the towns of the Amorites, is somewhat anticipatory of the history itself, as the settlement did not occur till Moses gave the conquered land to the tribes of Reuben and Gad for a possession (Num 32). The only places mentioned here are <hi type="italic">Heshbon</hi> and her daughters, i.e., the smaller towns belonging to it (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.13.17">Jos 13:17</reference>), which are enumerated singly in Num 32:34-38, and <reference osisRef="Josh.13.15">Jos 13:15</reference>-28. In explanation of the expression, “Heshbon and her daughters,” it is added in Num 21:26, that Heshbon was the city, i.e., the capital of the Amorite king Sihon, who had made war upon the former king of Moab, and taken away all his land as far as the Arnon. Consequently, even down to the time of the predecessor of Balak, the king of the Moabites at that time, the land to the north of the Arnon, and probably even as far as the lower Jabbok, to which point the kingdom of Sihon extended (see <reference osisRef="Deut.3.12-Deut.3.13">Deu 3:12-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference>), belonged to the Moabites. And in accordance with this, the country where the Israelites encamped opposite to Jericho, before crossing the Jordan, is reckoned as part of the land of Moab (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.5">Deu 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.29.1">Deu 29:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.49">Deu 32:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.34.5-Deut.34.6">Deu 34:5-6</reference>), and called Arboth Moab (see Num 22:1); whilst the women who seduced the Israelites to join in the idolatrous worship of Baal Peor are called daughters of Moab (Num 25:1).
entries.1f91ac007a7140d731342b1eb47fcb681fbc3512: Num 21:27-28 <div eID="gen1891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1892" type="x-p"/> The glorious conquest and destruction of the capital of the powerful king of the Amorites, in the might of the Lord their God, inspired certain composers of proverbs (משׁלים <hi type="italic">denom</hi>. from משׁל) to write songs in commemoration of the victory. Three strophes are given from a song of this kind, and introduced with the words “<hi type="italic">therefore</hi>,' sc., because Heshbon had fallen in this manner, “<hi type="italic">the composers of</hi> <hi type="italic">proverbs say.”</hi> The first strophe (Num 21:27 and Num 21:28) runs thus: “<hi type="italic">Come to Heshbon: Built and</hi> <hi type="italic">restored be the city of Sihon! For fire went out of Heshbon; flames from the city of Sihon. It devoured Ar Moab, the lords of the heights of Arnon.”</hi> The summons to come to Heshbon and build this ruined city up again, was not addressed to the Israelites, but to the conquered Amorites, and is to be interpreted as ironical (<hi type="italic">F. v. Meyer; Ewald, Gesch</hi>. ii. pp. 267, 268): “<hi type="italic">Come to Heshbon, ye victorious Amorites, and build your royal city up again, which we have laid in ruins! A fire has gone out of it, and burned up Ar Moab, and the lords of the heights of the Arnon.”</hi> The reference is to the war-fire, which the victorious Amorites kindled from Heshbon in the land of Moab under the former king of Moab; that is to say, the war in which they subjugated Ar Moab and the possessors of the heights of Arnon. <hi type="italic">Ar Moab</hi> (see at Num 21:15) appears to have been formerly the capital of all Moabitis, or at least of that portion of it which was situated upon the northern side of the Arnon; and the prominence given to it in <reference osisRef="Deut.2.9">Deu 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.18">Deu 2:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.29">Deu 2:29</reference>, is in harmony with this. The heights of Arnon are mentioned as the limits to which Sihon had carried his victorious supremacy over Moab. The “<hi type="italic">lords”</hi> of these heights are the Moabites.
entries.68daf5b1608e88dd1788ab7eab1c90fd93c97333: Num 21:29 <div eID="gen1892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1893" type="x-p"/> Second strophe: “<hi type="italic">Woe to thee, Moab! Thou art lost, people of Chemosh! He has given up his sons as fugitives, and his daughters into captivity-To Sihon, king of the Amorites.”</hi> The poet here turns to Moab, and announces its overthrow. <hi type="italic">Chemosh</hi> (כּמושׁ, from כּמושׁ = כּבשׁ, <hi type="italic">subactor, domitor</hi>) was the leading deity of the Moabites (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.7">Jer 48:7</reference>) as well as of the Ammonites (Jdg 11:24), and related not only to <hi type="italic">Milcom</hi>, a god of the Ammonites, but also to the early Canaanitish deity <hi type="italic">Baal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Moloch</hi>. According to a statement of <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> (on <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1-Isa.15.9">Isa 15:1-9</reference>), it was only another name for <hi type="italic">Baal Peor</hi>, probably a god of the sun, which was worshipped as the king of his nation and the god of war. He is found in this character upon the coins of <hi type="italic">Areopolis</hi>, standing upon a column, with a sword in his right hand and a lance and shield in the left, and with two fire-torches by his side (cf. <hi type="italic">Ekhel doctr. numm. vet. iii</hi>. p. 504), and was appeased by the sacrifice of children in times of great distress (2Ki 3:27). Further information, and to some extent a different view, are found in the article by <hi type="italic">J. G. Müller</hi> in <hi type="italic">Herzog's</hi> Cyclopaedia. The subject to נתן is neither Moab nor Jehovah, but Chemosh. The thought is this: as Chemosh, the god of Moab, could not deliver his people from the Amorite king; so now that Israel has conquered the latter, Moab is utterly lost. In the triumph which Israel celebrated over Moab through conquering its conquerors, there is a forewarning expressed of the ultimate subjection of Moab under the sceptre of Israel.
entries.1b72fa3be9dfbf63c46d47971281ce7aea9fd220: Num 21:30 <hi type="italic">Third strophe</hi>, in which the woe evoked upon Moab is justified: “<hi type="italic">We cast them down:</hi> <hi type="italic">Heshbon is lost even to Dibon; and we laid it waste even to Nophah, with fire to</hi> <hi type="italic">Medeba</hi>.” ונּירם is the first pers. pl. imperf. Kal of ירה with the suffix ־ם for ־ם (as in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.30">Exo 29:30</reference>). ירה, to cast arrows, to shoot down (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.13">Exo 19:13</reference>): figuratively to throw to the ground (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.4">Exo 15:4</reference>). נשּׁים for נשּׁם, first <hi type="italic">pers. pl. imperf</hi>. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of נשׁה, synonymous with נצה, Jer 4:7. The suffixes of both verbs refer to the Moabites as the inhabitants of the cities named. Accordingly <hi type="italic">Heshbon</hi> also is construed as a masculine, because it was not the town as such, but the inhabitants, that were referred to. <hi type="italic">Heshbon</hi>, the residence of king Sihon, stood pretty nearly in the centre between the Arnon and the Jabbok (according to the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. twenty Roman miles from the Jordan, opposite to Jericho), and still exists in extensive ruins with deep bricked wells, under the old name of <hi type="italic">Hesbân</hi> (cf. <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> p. 262). On <hi type="italic">Dibon</hi> in the south, not more than an hour from Arnon. <hi type="italic">Nophach</hi> is probably the same as <hi type="italic">Nobach</hi>, Jdg 8:11, but not the same as <hi type="italic">Kenath</hi>, which was altered into <hi type="italic">Nobach</hi> (Num 32:42). According to Jdg 8:11, it was near Jogbeha, not far from the eastern desert; and in all probability it still exists in the ruined place called <hi type="italic">Nowakis</hi> (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, p. 619; <hi type="italic">Buckingham</hi>, ii. p. 46; Robinson, App. p. 188), to the north-west of <hi type="italic">Ammân (Rabbath-Ammon)</hi>. <hi type="italic">Nophach</hi>, therefore, is referred to as a north-eastern town or fortress, and contrasted with <hi type="italic">Dibon</hi>, which was in the south. The words which follow, עד מ אשׁר, “<hi type="italic">which to Medeba,”</hi> yield no intelligible meaning. The Seventy give πῦρ ἐπὶ Μ. (fire upon Medeba), and seem to have adopted the reading עד אשׁ. In the Masoretic punctuation also, the ר in אשׁר is marked as suspicious by a <hi type="italic">punct.</hi> <hi type="italic">extraord</hi>. Apparently, therefore, אשׁר was a copyist’s error of old standing for אשׁ, and is to be construed as governed by the verb נשּׁים, “with fire to <hi type="italic">Medeba</hi>.” The city was about two hours to the south-east of Heshbon, and is still to be seen in ruins bearing the name of <hi type="italic">Medaba</hi>, upon the top of a hill of about half-an-hour’s journey in circumference (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, p. 625; <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> pp. 264-5).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> and <hi type="italic">Bleek</hi> (Einleitung in d. A. T. p. 200) are both agreed that this ode was composed on the occasion of the defeat of the Amorites by the Israelites, and particularly on the capture of the capital Heshbon, as it depicts the fall of Heshbon in the most striking way; and this city was rebuilt shortly afterwards by the Reubenites, and remained ever afterwards a city of some importance. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, on the other hand, has completely misunderstood the meaning and substance of the verses quoted, and follows some of the earliest commentators, such as <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi> and others, in regarding the ode as an Amoritish production, and interpreting it as relating to the conquest and fortification of Heshbon by Sihon.</note>
entries.4a38bf3e1c883844f9ff4ec74a5a6fba5fe69a42: Num 21:31-32 <div eID="gen1893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1894" type="x-p"/> When Israel was sitting, i.e., encamped, in the land of the Amorites, Moses reconnoitred <hi type="italic">Jaezer</hi>, after which the Israelites took “its daughters,” i.e., the smaller places dependent upon Jaezer, and destroyed the Amorites who dwelt in them. It is evident from Num 32:35, that Jaezer was not only conquered, but destroyed. This city, which was situated, according to the Onom. (<hi type="italic">s. v. Jazer</hi>), ten Roman miles to the west of <hi type="italic">Philadelphia (Rabbath-Ammon)</hi>, and fifteen Roman miles to the north of Heshbon, is most probably to be sought for (as <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi> supposes, i. pp. 397, 406, iv. p. 216) in the ruins of <hi type="italic">es Szîr</hi>, at the source of the <hi type="italic">Nahr Szîr</hi>, in the neighbourhood of which <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi> found some pools, which are probably the remains of “the sea of Jazer,” mentioned in Jer 48:32. There is less probability in <hi type="italic">Burckhardt's</hi> conjecture, that it is to be found in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Ain Hazir</hi>, near <hi type="italic">Kherbet el Suk</hi>, to the south-west of <hi type="italic">es Salt</hi>; though <hi type="italic">v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Raumer</hi> (<hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> p. 262) decides in its favour (see my Commentary on <reference osisRef="Josh.13.25">Jos 13:25</reference>).
entries.d00b11ba5af1069c2881c40085456720c5794fce: Num 21:33-35 <div eID="gen1894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1895" type="x-p"/> The Israelites then turned towards the north, and took the road to Bashan, where king Og came against them with his people, to battle at <hi type="italic">Edrei</hi>. From what point it was that the Israelites entered upon the expedition against Bashan, is not stated either here or in Deu 3:1., where Moses recapitulates these events, and gives a more detailed account of the conquests than he does here, simply because it was of no importance in relation to the main object of the history. We have probably to picture the conquest of the kingdoms of Sihon and Og as taking place in the following manner: namely, that after Sihon had been defeated at Jahza, and his capital had been speedily taken in consequence of this victory, Moses sent detachments of his army from the places of encampment mentioned in Num 21:16, Num 21:18-20, into the different divisions of his kingdom, for the purpose of taking possession of their towns. After the conquest of the whole of the territory of Sihon, the main army advanced to Bashan and defeated king Og in a great battle at Edrei, whereupon certain detachments of the army were again despatched, under courageous generals, to secure the conquest of the different parts of his kingdom (cf. Num 32:39, Num 32:41-42). The kingdom of Og embraced the northern half of Gilead, i.e., the country between the Jabbok and the Mandhur (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.13">Deu 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference>), the modern Jebel <hi type="italic">Ajlun</hi>, and “all Bashan,” or “all the region of <hi type="italic">Argob</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.4">Deu 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.13-Deut.3.14">Deu 3:13-14</reference>), the modern plain of <hi type="italic">Jaulan</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hauran</hi>, which extended eastwards to <hi type="italic">Salcah</hi>, north-eastwards to <hi type="italic">Edrei</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.10">Deu 3:10</reference>), and northwards to <hi type="italic">Geshur</hi> and <hi type="italic">Maacha</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference>). For further remarks, see Deu 3:10. There were two towns in Bashan of the name of <hi type="italic">Edrei</hi>. One of them, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.1.4">Deu 1:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.12.4">Jos 12:4</reference>, along with <hi type="italic">Ashtaroth</hi>, as a second residence of king Og, is described in the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. (<hi type="italic">s. v. Ashtaroth and Edrei</hi>) as six Roman miles, i.e., fully two hours, from Ashtaroth, and twenty-four or twenty-five miles from Bostra, and called <hi type="italic">Adraa</hi> or <hi type="italic">Adara</hi>. This is the modern <hi type="italic">Derà</hi> or <hi type="italic">Draà</hi> (in <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, p. 385; <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, i. pp. 363, 364), and <hi type="italic">Draah, Idderat</hi> (in <hi type="italic">Buckingham, Syr. ii</hi>. p. 146), a place which still exists, consisting of a number of miserable houses, built for the most part of basalt, and standing upon a small elevation in a treeless, hilly region, with the ruins of an old church and other smaller buildings, supposed to belong to the time when <hi type="italic">Draa,</hi> <hi type="italic">Adraa</hi> (as <hi type="italic">urbs Arabiae</hi>), was an episcopal see, on the east of the pilgrim-road between <hi type="italic">Remtha</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mezareib</hi>, by the side of a small wady (see <hi type="italic">Ritter, Erdk</hi>. xv. pp. 838ff.). The other <hi type="italic">Edrei</hi>, which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Deut.3.10">Deu 3:10</reference> as the north-western frontier of Bashan, was farther towards the north, and is still to be seen in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Zorah</hi> or <hi type="italic">Ethra</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.3.10">Deu 3:10</reference>). In the present instance the southern town is intended, which was not far from the south-west frontier of Bashan, as Og certainly did not allow the Israelites to advance to the northern frontier of his kingdom before he gave them battle.

entries.9ede509d994346391bc809f496504e5dd4cef948: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.21.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.21.1" sID="gen20146" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen20147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">And when king Arad the Canaanite.</hi> It is not altogether agreed among commentators who this king Arad was. Some think that he was an Amalekite, but this error is refuted by the fact that the Amalekites had already attempted in vain to interrupt the journey of the people. Nor is it credible that after so great a slaughter, they would have endeavored to do so again, especially since their territories remained untouched. Besides, it would have been absurd to call the Amalekites Canaanites, since they derived their origin not from Canaan but from Esau, and thus were connected with the Israelites by a common descent from Shem. We shall, however, rightly understand this as referring to the Amorites, who were certainly reckoned among the Canaanites, as being of the same race; as Moses tells us in his first book, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.16">Genesis 10:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.21">Genesis 15:21</reference>;) nay, he elsewhere designates all the people of Canaan by the name of Amorites. Moreover, in the thirty-fourth chapter of this book, we shall see that their boundaries reached to mount Hor and Kadesh-barnea. Since, then, the Amorites were in this neighborhood towards the south, the name will suit them very well. That king Arad, however, alone made war upon them, arose from the paternal providence of God, who wished to accustom His people to the conquest of their enemies by degrees. If all these nations had united their forces, and made a combined attack upon an unwarlike people, it would have succumbed in astonishment and fear. But it was easier for them to defend themselves against a single nation. And yet, in the first combat, God permitted the Israelites to be routed, so that the victorious Canaanite took some booty, or led away some captives. And this also was useful to the Israelites, in order that, mistrusting their own strength, they might humbly betake themselves to the succor of God; for it behooved them to learn that, unless they were aided from on high, they would be altogether insufficient, when they had to resist many powerful nations, since they had not been able to withstand even a single people.<div eID="gen20147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20148" type="x-p"/>With respect to “the way of the spies,” some understand that, as the people had been taught by Joshua and Caleb, they followed the footsteps of those who had been sent to explore the land; but, inasmuch as it appears that the course was a different one, I know not whether this opinion is very tenable. Thus, some take the word <foreign xml:lang="he">דרך</foreign>, <hi type="italic">derek, to </hi>mean “after the manner of,” <note n="116"> <div sID="gen20149" type="x-p"/> It is again <hi type="italic">S.M.</hi> who has mentioned this opinion. — <hi type="italic">W.</hi><div eID="gen20149" type="x-p"/> </note> which appears to be harsh and constrained. Thus, then, I explain it, Since they had to advance through unknown regions, spies were sent on, according to custom, to direct the whole march; and hence king Arad knew that his territory was to be invaded, before the army had proceeded so far.<div eID="gen20148" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.21.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen20146" osisID="Num.21.1" type="section"/>
entries.3cfacb58a643699c799e0582ed62dfd3562a7ca7:
2. And Israel vowed a vow unto the Lord. This was a manifestation of piety, when they had sustained a loss, not to cast away hope, nor to murmur against God; but to encourage themselves by entreating His aid. To this slate of submissiveness they had been subdued by the chastisements of God, although the continuance of their obedience, as we shall presently see, was not of long duration. Any one at first sight would say that there was something absurd in this vow; but we gather from the result, that it was lawful and approved by God; for the sign of His approbation was that tie hearkened to the vows and cry of the people. I admit, indeed, that God sometimes answers defective prayers, but there is no doubt whatever but that Moses here commends their piety in the vow. We must consider, then, how it was lawful for them to offer the destruction of cities and the wasting of lands to God as a sacrifice of sweet savor; and the reply to this question will be easy, if we bear in mind that the vow did not originate in inconsiderate zeal, but rather in the command of God. It seems cruel to destroy an entire nation; but God had not only decreed its destruction, but had appointed the Israelites to execute His sentence. Hence the vow, of which we are now treating, was not idly spoken, being founded on God’s word, which is the first rule for vowing rightly. It was, indeed, allowable for them to spare the cities, in order to possess them themselves; but it was also allowable to devote them as an offering (in anathema) of first-fruits to God, as we are elsewhere told of the city of Jericho. This at any rate we must conclude, that although God had not openly and expressly commanded the cities to be utterly destroyed, still this vow was dictated by the Holy Spirit, lest the people should yield to sloth, and set themselves down in a single corner, but that, having desolated and wasted this region, they might encourage themselves the more to further progress. The vero חרם charam, which Moses employs, signifies, indeed, to destroy, and from it is derived the word, חרמה chormah, or Hormah, which implies a species of anathema, as if they devoted the land to the curse of God. Moses, however, adds, that the people performed the vow, under the obligation of which they had laid themselves; and praiseworthy indeed was their magnanimity, in refusing to avail themselves of a comfortable home by destroying the cities, which they had acquired by the right of war.
We know not whether the cities were destroyed immediately after the victory over their enemies; indeed, I rather conjecture that there was some interval of time, because the people did not straightway enter the boundaries of the promised land. And this more clearly appears from chapter 33, where, after this battle was fought, certain stations are enumerated, which are in another direction. It is probable, therefore, that they fought outside the boundaries of the Canaanites, and that, when the people came here soon afterwards, the land was finally put to the sword.
